t: Minimum Subarray Length With Distinct Sum At Least K
o: Find the shortest contiguous subarray where the sum of its distinct values (each counted once) is ≥ k. In [2,2,3,1] with k=4 the window [2,3] works (distinct sum 5, length 2); in [3,2,3,4] with k=5 the window [3,2] works; in [5,5,4] with k=5 a single [5] works. Distinct sum is monotone under expansion/shrinkage of a window (adding an element never decreases it, removing never increases), so a two-pointer sweep with frequency counts applies.
k: Track the distinct-value sum incrementally: add a value when its count goes 0→1, subtract when it goes 1→0.
For each right endpoint, shrink the left while the distinct sum stays ≥ k, recording the minimal window.

a.i: Expand r, maintaining cnt[value] and dsum = sum of values with cnt > 0. While dsum ≥ k, the window [l, r] is a candidate; shrink from the left to seek shorter valid windows. Monotonicity guarantees each pointer moves at most n times.
s: Initialize cnt map, dsum = 0, l = 0, ans = infinity.
For each r: if cnt[nums[r]] == 0 add nums[r] to dsum; increment cnt.
While dsum ≥ k: update ans with r-l+1; decrement cnt[nums[l]], subtracting the value if its count hits 0; advance l.
Return ans or -1 if never updated.
a.t: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window at most once; map operations amortized O(1)
a.sp: O(n) — frequency map in the worst case of all-distinct values

w: The monotonicity argument is the heart: prove distinct-sum responds monotonically to window growth/shrink before committing to two pointers. Pitfall: updating dsum on duplicates incorrectly (only 0↔1 transitions matter), and forgetting the -1 case. Note the answer window need not be minimal by ordinary sum. Follow-up: longest such subarray, or distinct sum bounded both below and above.
